content_html:
Blyg going by the description here is much closer to Zettelkasten method. The key difference is that each post is identified by timestamp. At human scale, combined with DNS, it is unique.

How to Blyg

I think the key shift is: don’t ask “what topics should I post about?” Ask “what units of thought deserve an address?”

Blygger changes the natural unit of publication. A fragment is not a tiny essay. It is an addressable semantic object: it has identity, history, provenance, and can later be transcluded into multiple larger constructions. The protocol explicitly separates atomic fragments from threads composed by transclusion, while preserving which version was incorporated.

That suggests a very different publishing practice.

Post moves, not subjects

Your subjects are already abundant: protocols, thickets, Prime Radiant, AI, capitalism, geography, writing, institutions, history. Trying to come up with more subjects will probably slow you down.

Instead, publish whenever you make one intellectual move:

  • A distinction: “Protocols optimize for available moves; products optimize for outcomes.”
  • A connection: “Hayekian price signals and protocol constraints may be structurally similar.”
  • A named phenomenon: “Functional fixedness in writing begins when you title the thought.”
  • An observation: “AI seems to make software ecosystems around individuals economically viable.”
  • A question: “What happens when a protocol becomes easier to fork than to govern?”
  • A contradiction: “Self-sovereignty increases freedom but may decrease legibility.”
  • A metaphor: “A personal AI-built software environment is less like an app suite than a biome.”
  • A small empirical finding: something that happened while building Blygger, Prime Radiant, your blog, or working with AI that surprised you.
  • A revision: “I previously thought X. I now think the more important variable is Y.”

The threshold I’d use is:

Would I want to be able to point to this exact thought six months from now?

If yes, it deserves an ID.

That is much lower than the traditional blogging threshold of “Do I have enough to say?”

And that lower threshold is not merely a convenience. It changes what kind of thinking becomes possible.

The deeper effect is decomposition without loss of identity

Ordinary note-taking decomposes thought, but the fragments are private and usually disappear into later prose.

Ordinary blogging preserves identity, but at the level of the essay.

Twitter gives individual thoughts identity, but largely fixes their meaning to a moment in a stream.

Blygger does something stranger: it gives the pre-essay thought a durable public identity.

Suppose you publish:

F17: “AI allows an individual to build an ecosystem around their own idiosyncrasies.”

Today that might occur to you while thinking about personal software.

Three months later you might use F17 in a thread about protocols.

Six months later it might appear in something about craftsmanship.

Later still, perhaps it becomes relevant to your idea of the thicket.

The important thing is that these are not four copies of the sentence. They’re four uses of the same intellectual object.

That’s where the multidimensionality you are sensing comes from.

An essay essentially says:

A → B → C → D → E

The author determines the path.

A collection of independently addressable fragments can instead become something like a hypergraph:

         Protocols
         /      \
       F17 —— F31
      /  \       \
    AI   Thicket  Capital
     \     |
      \   F52
       \ /
    Personal computing

A thread is then one traversal through the graph, rather than the container in which the ideas permanently live.

This is a profound inversion.

The essay stops being the fundamental object. The idea becomes fundamental.

And this explains why you should resist finishing fragments

Rao recently made an observation about Blygger that gets very close to this. He noted that even titling a thought can impose “functional fixedness”: declaring it to be about X suppresses possible associations with things that aren’t X. His term for the desirable opposite is “stem-celliness”—leave thoughts semantically undifferentiated until there’s a reason to specialize them.

I think that’s one of the most important emergent properties of the medium.

Your instinct may be to improve:

Capitalism becomes a force of nature when its externalities become planetary.

into:

Capitalism, Climate and Natural Feedback Loops

Capitalism has traditionally…

Don’t.

The first thing has more potential energy.

It can become part of an essay on capitalism, climate, Hayek, cybernetics, ecology, governance, feedback systems, or the distinction between culture and nature.

The second has already collapsed the wavefunction.

So there are really two kinds of Blygger writing

I’d think of them as stem cells and organisms.

Fragments should retain optionality.

Threads expend optionality to make an argument.

And critically, the organism does not consume the stem cell. Because transclusion preserves the fragment’s identity, the same fragment remains available for an entirely different organism later. Blygger’s versioning makes this more powerful still: the fragment itself can develop over time without silently rewriting what earlier threads quoted.

So your publishing loop becomes:

notice → publish → notice → publish → connect → revise → compose

rather than:

research → outline → draft → edit → publish

That first loop should be dramatically faster.

This also changes what “thinking in public” means

Most thinking-in-public systems are really showing unfinished work.

This is subtly different.

You’re creating public intellectual components.

That gives other people—or AIs—a different affordance. They don’t have to respond to the argument as a whole. They can grab F17, combine it with one of their own fragments, disagree with F31, fork F52, or create a completely different traversal.

And because Blygger deliberately lacks a conventional reply primitive, response itself becomes publication: quote, transclude, fork, construct.

That’s much closer to combinatorial culture than social media.

You aren’t just increasing the number of utterances.

You’re increasing the number of possible future compositions.

And that leads me to a slightly different interpretation of your thicket metaphor.

An essay is a tree: trunk, branches, hierarchy, authorial direction.

A stream is a river: chronological, disappearing downstream.

A Blygger archive can actually become a thicket: persistent little things growing independently, crossing, grafting onto each other, becoming substrate for later growth, without any single privileged hierarchy.

That means the right posting strategy is almost the opposite of traditional blogging:

Publish things before you know what they’re for.

Not sloppy things. Not every passing reaction. But well-formed thoughts whose eventual role remains unresolved.

If I were adopting this seriously, I’d set myself one simple rule:

Whenever I notice a thought that makes one new distinction, connection, observation, question, or metaphor, and I would be annoyed if I couldn’t find it again, I blyg it.

Then every few weeks, don’t ask “What essay should I write?”

Ask:

“What structures have started appearing among these fragments?”

That’s where I suspect the real payoff is. The higher posting rate isn’t the objective. Density comes first; structure emerges afterward.

And unlike Twitter, where higher posting frequency mostly produces more stream, here higher fragment density should eventually produce a richer space of traversable thought. That is the experiment I think is worth running.
